column7: From Raja Harishchandra (1913) to the last silent films before Alam Ara (1931): every film made in India was silent, with intertitles in Hindi, English and other languages.
column11: Added 28 Nov 2026 (Amitabh, R2). Silent films carry no language of their own; the register counts them as Hindi cinema by their sources.

column7: From the first Hindi talkie, Alam Ara (1931), to Independence: studio-era films made in Bombay, Calcutta, Lahore and Poona, lavish romantic musicals and melodramas, with songs in almost every film.
column11: Sources group the 1930s and 1940s together; the end year 1946 is set by the golden age starting at Independence.

column7: From Independence to the mid 1960s, regarded by film historians as the golden age of Hindi cinema (Pyaasa, Awaara, Shree 420, Mother India, Mughal-e-Azam).
column11: Hindi cinema says late 1940s to early 1960s; Musical film says late 1940s to 1960s. End year 1964 is our choice between them.

column7: The late 1960s and early 1970s, when the industry was dominated by musical romance films with romantic-hero leads.
column11: One source only so far; ends where Classic Bollywood begins (Zanjeer and Yaadon Ki Baarat, 1973).

column7: The 1970s and 1980s, when the conventions of commercial Hindi film were set: the masala film, the angry young man, Salim-Javed, Amitabh Bachchan; the name Bollywood was coined.
column11: Starts 1973 (Zanjeer; Yaadon Ki Baarat, the first masala film, per Hindi cinema).

column7: Contemporary Bollywood since the early 1990s, linked to economic liberalisation: family romantic musicals, the Khans, the overseas market, multiplex and franchise films.

Art-house realism outside the commercial mainstream, often without song-and-dance routines: from Neecha Nagar and Dharti Ke Lal (1946) and Do Bigha Zamin (1953) to the Indian New Wave of Shyam Benegal, Mani Kaul, Kumar Shahani, Govind Nihalani.
column11: Peak in Hindi cinema in the 1970s and 1980s; sources note a resurgence at the end of the 1990s (Mumbai noir), kept as its own movement. Membership needs a film list.

column7: Gritty urban crime and action films around an anti-establishment hero, introduced by Salim-Javed with Zanjeer (1973) and Deewaar (1975), led by Amitabh Bachchan; the trend lasted into the early 1990s.
column11: One source; end year from "lasted into the early 1990s". Membership needs a film list.

column7: Films that blend action, comedy, romance and melodrama with songs, pioneered by Manmohan Desai, Prakash Mehra, Nasir Hussain and Salim-Javed; Yaadon Ki Baarat (1973) is called the first.
column11: Ongoing. Wikidata tags films with genre masala (P136) for some films only.

column7: Urban crime films reflecting the city's social problems, after the success of Satya (1998).
column11: One source. Wikidata Q114210202 is the crime-fiction genre, not the film movement, so it is not linked.

column7: Films catering to the Indian diaspora overseas, a phase Hindi cinema credits to Aditya Chopra and Karan Johar, with high production values (Kabhi Khushi Kabhie Gham, Kal Ho Naa Ho, Veer-Zaara).
column11: Source places it in the 2000s; many writers start it with Dilwale Dulhania Le Jayenge (1995). Needs your call on the start year. Start moved from 2000 to 1995 (Amitabh, 28 Nov 2026): Senses of Cinema (2022) dates the NRI genre from Dilwale Dulhania Le Jayenge (1995), Pardes and Kuch Kuch Hota Hai.

column7: The Golden Age of Hollywood: the studio system and the classical continuity style, from the coming of sound (The Jazz Singer, 1927) to the arrival of New Hollywood.
column11: Ends before Bonnie and Clyde and The Graduate (1967).

column7: The American New Wave: a film-school generation of directors (Coppola, Scorsese, Spielberg, Lucas, Altman) took the authorial role as the studio system declined.
column11: Sources say mid or late 1960s to early 1980s; end year 1980 is our choice.

column7: The modern blockbuster, high-concept franchises and special effects, alongside a growing independent film scene.
column11: One source; the start overlaps the end of New Hollywood (Jaws 1975, Star Wars 1977 are often named as its origin).

column7: Twenty-first century Hollywood: superhero and franchise dominance, digital production, then streaming and the end of the theatrical window.
Early sound films made before the Production Code was enforced (1 July 1934), with franker content.
column11: Start is "late 1920s" in the source; 1929 is used as the year sound became widespread.

column2: Golden age of the musical film
column7: From The Jazz Singer (1927) to the early 1950s, when the musical was at its most popular: Busby Berkeley, Astaire and Rogers, Judy Garland, Gene Kelly.
column11: Source: "the 1930s through the early 1950s"; 1954 is our end year. Includes films with musical numbers that are not full musicals only if their genre is musical.

column7: The production unit at MGM led by Arthur Freed that renewed the musical, from Meet Me in St. Louis (1944) to Easter Parade, On the Town, An American in Paris, Singin' in the Rain and Gigi.
column11: End year to confirm from Arthur Freed's filmography (Bells Are Ringing, 1960, is usually the last).

column7: Large-budget musicals from West Side Story (1961), My Fair Lady and The Sound of Music to the costly flops of the late 1960s and early 1970s.
column11: Start and end years read from the films the source names.

column7: Ten Walt Disney Feature Animation musicals from The Little Mermaid (1989) to Tarzan (1999), with songs by Howard Ashman, Alan Menken, Tim Rice and others.

column7: The revival of the film musical in the 21st century: Moulin Rouge!, Chicago, Dreamgirls, La La Land, jukebox musicals and music biopics.

Hindi films released straight to streaming services (Amazon Prime Video, Netflix, Disney+ Hotstar, ZEE5) instead of cinemas, a shift the 2020 pandemic closures made mainstream; Gulabo Sitabo went to Amazon Prime Video in June 2020.
column11: Added at Amitabh's request (27 Nov). The wave starts in 2020, so earlier streaming originals (from about 2018) stay outside it. Reads the original broadcaster (Wikidata P449) or a streaming distributor.

column7: Films made for or released first on American streaming platforms (Netflix, Disney+, Paramount+, Apple TV+), which came to rival cinemas from 2019 and ended the 90-day theatrical window during the pandemic.
